newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania president urges faster government reforms.
newsitem.headline: Romania president urges faster government reforms.

text.p: President Emil Constantinescu urged Romania's centrist government on Friday to speed up the restructuring of inefficient industry and produce a revised 1997 budget or face a mass reshuffle.

"There will be no backtracking from this (reform) line. Should this happen, I will intervene," the independent Mediafax news agency quoted Constantinescu as saying as ministers examined proposed revisions to meet IMF demands.
"A government that doesn't carry out reforms has no reason for existence. In such a case, I will propose a government reshuffle or the whole government will have to go."

An International Monetary Fund mission has been in Romania since mid-July to assess progress in implementing overdue reforms launched earlier this year. It has made no public comment on the government's performance.
Revising the budget and establishing new targets for economic indicators are the IMF's main conditions for releasing the second of five $86 million loan tranches.

Ministers have pledged to keep the budget deficit to within earlier targets of 4.5 percent of gross domestic product but admit that the initial objective of 90 percent inflation for 1997 has long been dashed by large price rises in the spring.
Seven hours into a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, a government official said the revisions would win final approval next week.
A Western banking source said despite public bickering among ministers defending their budget allocations, he was optimistic agreement acceptable to the IMF would be achieved.
"Things are going well," he said. "There will be meetings through the weekend. We should have something by mid-week."

The government decided on Friday to postpone for two more weeks the liquidation of Romania's state-run oil company, a creation of its leftist predecessor. Three options on how to replace the bloated refining industry were to be considered.
On Thursday, Romania's biggest trade unions seeking wage indexation and tax cuts walked out of talks with Ciorbea and accused ministers of botching reform.
Constantinescu travels on Saturday to the western Jiu Valley coalfield to mark the 20th anniversary of a rare miners' uprising against communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Trade unionists have generally supported Constantinescu's reforms apart from sporadic protests, including some led by the Jiu Valley miners last month.
The reformist president has criticised ministers' failure to slim down communist-era industry and suggested that some had not been doing their jobs. But he has stood by Ciorbea.

Ciorbea's government of Christian Democrats, Liberals, Social Democrats and members of the 1.6 million-strong ethnic Hungarian community was appointed after last year's centrist election victory over former communists.
It has freed prices -- which triggered long suppressed inflation -- as well as revamped foreign exchange markets and introduced laws to attract foreign investors.

Monthly inflation, which peaked at more than 30 percent in March, is expected to slide below two percent in July. But economists say Romania's inflation could still end up as high as 150 percent by the end of the year.
